source.title: Training against the monitor: What happens during Obfuscated Adversarial Training?

record.tranche_reason: Conceptually tests whether a monitor-detectable harmfulness signal can be present when generated behavior is non-harmful, using trained linear probes and output scoring rather than the original difference-in-means refusal direction.
record.gate_note: The study analyzes OAT-trained harmful-versus-benign probes and monitor evasion, not the original single refusal direction. It does not test refusal-direction ablation or addition, a weight edit intended to remove refusal, or refusal rates after an intervention. The V5 rows capture the reported probe-versus-generation dissociation. Other mechanistic measurements, including LoRA subspace capture, writer decompositions, and KL changes, do not directly measure the versions in this claim and are not catalogued as rows.
record.test_reason: The study analyses Obfuscated Adversarial Training (OAT) harmfulness probes and embedding attacks that evade them. It never finds, ablates, adds or edits a refusal direction, and it reports no refusal rates under any refusal-direction intervention. The probes are externally trained harmful-vs-benign monitors. The adapters were trained to keep those probes working, so probe signal is a related but different construct from the model's own harm judgment or refusal decision. The clean-prompt rows (r1–r6) show harmful requests detected while the model refuses. Detection and refusal co-occur there, which is no dissociation of harm from refusal, so they do not test V5. The closest V5-relevant result is that behaviour-only attacks give harmful output while the probe still detects 100%. That is a trained monitor's persistence under attack on OAT checkpoints, not a measurement of how the model separates harm from refusal.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly correct. The authors conclude that OAT checkpoints contain a causally active, probe-aligned, near-rank-1 writer component inside a distributed reader–writer circuit. Stronger probe-aware embedding attacks suppress or bypass that signal, reaching 0 detections at StrongREJECT about 0.81. OAT raises the attack budget needed but does not give robustness. They frame this as a single-seed mechanistic case study, not a general OAT result.
record.recipe_differences: Uses six frozen linear probes trained to classify harmful versus benign examples, OAT LoRA adapters, and embedding attacks; it does not find the original difference-in-means refusal direction or project that direction out of every layer and position.
record.method_sensitivity: Attack optimization budget changes probe scores and detection; the study reports different outcomes for 1B and 3B checkpoints and for probe-targeted versus behaviour-only attacks.

fits_no_version.finding: Probe-targeted embedding attacks at 256 PGD steps cut OAT harmfulness-probe detection to 0% while StrongREJECT stayed around 0.81 in both checkpoints.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Sufficiently optimized embedding attacks evade OAT-hardened harmfulness probes while keeping harmful generations.

fits_no_version.finding: On clean harmful prompts the model mostly refuses (StrongREJECT 0.048/0.091), yet the probe flags 95–100% of them. The probe responds to request intent, not to harmful assistance.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Harmfulness probes on generation tokens track harmful request context regardless of whether the model complies.

fits_no_version.finding: Behaviour-only attacks gave high StrongREJECT (0.80–0.85) while probe detection stayed at 100% at every budget. No row records this.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Harmful compliance induced without probe pressure leaves the harmfulness-probe signal intact in OAT checkpoints.

fits_no_version.finding: Removing the probe-parallel part of the writer LoRA-B matrices lowers generated probe scores, against a norm-matched random control.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: OAT checkpoints contain a causally active, probe-aligned writer component that adds monitor-visible signal.

record.problems: One trained adapter and probe per model size; no matched non-OAT, warmup, or standard-LoRA controls; the same 20 harmful and 20 benign prompts are reused; only greedy generations and a model-graded StrongREJECT score are used, with no human evaluation. The authors also state that the results do not establish generalization across seeds, model families, monitors, or attack families.
record.rows_left_out: No rows were retained for the remaining attack budgets, behavior-only controls, writer-ablation scopes, or other mechanistic experiments because they concern OAT harmfulness-monitor behavior rather than any tested claim version. The reported 0%/high-StrongREJECT result at 256 steps is retained for both models.

untested.parts: No difference-in-means refusal direction; no ablation or addition; no refusal or capability outcomes.
No weight edit to remove refusal.
Attacks target harmfulness probes, not a refusal direction; no ablation-based adversarial training.
No multi-direction or cone analysis of refusal. The near-rank-1 writer concerns probe signal in LoRA adapters, not refusal.
No separation of the model's own harm representation from its refusal decision; only an external, OAT-trained monitor is used.

record.verdict_notes: The reader's V5 'supports' label is removed. Probe detection plus refusal on clean prompts shows no harm/refusal dissociation, and the probe is an external monitor trained under OAT, not the model's refusal mechanism. The study does not cite or test the refusal-direction work.

versions.untested_parts: No difference-in-means refusal direction is found or ablated across layers and positions; no addition intervention, refusal outcome, or general-capability check of that intervention.
No refusal-removing weight edit or released-model abliteration evaluation.
Attacks optimize against six harmfulness probes, not the claimed refusal direction; the study does not test training against ablation of that direction for robustness.
No comparison of affine, cone, single-direction, or multi-direction accounts of refusal.

The study compares an externally trained harmful-versus-benign activation probe with generated-response harmfulness scores; it does not directly elicit the model's own harmfulness judgment or causally separate that judgment from its refusal decision.
No cross-language or base-to-instruct transfer test.

Only one OAT-style adapter and probe training seed per model size is studied; there are no matched non-OAT or training-stage controls to test how training determines whether a removable refusal direction exists.

relation.should_be: none (no listed category fits; nearest is cites_only, but there is no citation)
relation.reason: The text never mentions a refusal direction, Arditi et al., abliteration or difference-in-means. Its only remark about refusal says the probe detects harmful intent even when the model refuses (Exp. 7). That remark interprets its own probe, not the claim.

tranche.reason: The study never finds, ablates, adds or edits a refusal direction. Its probes are OAT-hardened harmfulness monitors reading generation-token activations, and its results bear on monitor evasion, not on any version. The behaviour-only result (StrongREJECT about 0.85 with 100% detection) is close to V5, but OAT trains for it and no refusal direction is measured.

source_check.notes: Every value comes from a single-seed OAT LoRA checkpoint with no non-OAT control. The author says this means OAT can't be confirmed as the cause. n is 20 harmful prompts (60 generations per model per budget across 3 attack inits). The authors_conclusion paraphrase is accurate.

reader_labels.label: supports
reader_labels.condition: Clean harmful prompts on the two tested instruct checkpoints
reader_labels.reason: The probes detected harmful prompts at high rates while generated outputs had low StrongREJECT scores described as consistent with refusal (r1–r6).
